records.query: Explain the use of the Grade 2 coating for special-purpose trucks and how the coating is used differently for forklifts.
records.reference: For special-purpose trucks, Grade 2 coating is used to protect seams, joints, and exterior metal-to-metal connections, such as around window areas, hinges, and ladder pipe rail welds. For forklifts, Grade 2 is applied to the hoist chain, sprockets, mast rollers, hose reels, and all surface metal-to-metal joints. It is also used to spray a light film over the entire exterior surface and both sides of all wheels, rims, and lugs. The key difference is that for forklifts, Grade 2 is applied to the exterior surface and wheels, whereas for special-purpose trucks, it is used on specific seams and joints.
records.answer:
Grade 2 is a light corrosion-preventive coating used on special-purpose vehicles (and general vehicles) in TO 36-1-191 for exterior and metal-to-metal protection. On special-purpose vehicle instruction sheets, Grade 2 is applied to: window seams, side door hinges, inner compartments and all metal-to-metal joints; the entire exterior surface as a light coating (wipe or polish off excess with a clean cloth if the film is too heavy); and both sides of wheels, rims and lugs. On full-tracked special-purpose vehicles it is also used on cable, pulleys and crane cab seams and floor areas.

For forklifts, Grade 2 is used differently: it is applied to the hoist chain, sprockets and mast rollers, hose reels, and all surface metal-to-metal joints; a light film is sprayed over the entire exterior surface (wiping or polishing off excess if too heavy); both sides of all wheels, rims and lugs; and the exterior surface of floor plates. Forklift underside, closed-in and boxed-in areas get Grade 1 instead, and Grade 4 is used on the electrical system, while Grade 3 is used for radiator electrolysis control.

Note: the pages read cover special-purpose (full-tracked) vehicles and general purpose vehicles; no page explicitly defined Grade 2 as a standalone term.

records.query: What hazards can occur during F-18 hot refueling, and what steps should be taken to minimize the risk related to tank pressure and fuel spills?
records.reference: Hazards during F-18 hot refueling include fire, fuel leaks, fuel spillage, injury or death to personnel, and long-term health hazards. Steps to minimize risk related to tank pressure and fuel spills include monitoring fuel vents on the vertical stabilizers, ensuring the bullet plug is properly aligned, securing the refueling nozzle, and avoiding hazardous areas like the tail hook zone.
records.answer:
Hazards and mitigation for F-18 (F/A-18 A/B/C/D) hot refueling, per TO 00-25-172CL-3 Chapter 5:

Hazards:
- Tank overpressure: the SPR panel has a tank pressure gauge with a green safe zone and a red danger zone. Stopping at the red zone is required to avoid injury, death, or long-term health hazards.
- Fuel spills from the vertical stabilizer fuel dump/vent outlets, which can cause injury, death, or long-term health hazards.
- Fuel spill from the VENT TANK WET condition (F-18C/D only), which can spill fuel from the vent outlet(s).
- Fuel spill if the bullet plug is not properly seated (do not proceed).
- Nozzle coming off the SPR while the system is pressurized (verify the nozzle is locked before pressurizing).

Steps to minimize risk:
- Before refueling: stop at least 50 ft short of the hot refueling area; check for hot brakes; verify external tanks and stores are safed; set the external fuel tank safety select to LOCKED; verify the fuel dump (jettison) valve is closed; verify the external tank fueling switch is OFF.
- Before pressurizing the fuel source: attempt to remove the nozzle with the flow handle open; if it comes off, do not start refueling until the nozzle is replaced.
- Pre-check: hold both pre-check valves open; fuel flow should stop within 20 seconds, otherwise discontinue hot refueling. On F-18C/D, press VENT TANK SNSR TEST and confirm the VENT TANK WET light illuminates; if it does not, do not hot refuel. Fuel flow should stop 10 to 30 seconds after the external tank pre-check switches are pressed; if not, discontinue.
- During refueling: monitor the fuel vents on the vertical stabilizers and stop fuel flow if fuel spills from either vent outlet. Monitor the tank pressure gauge and stop all refueling flow if it shows red. Check for air flowing from the external tank vents as tanks fill. On F-18C/D, if the VENT TANK WET light illuminates, immediately discontinue hot refueling.
- After fueling: when flow stops, shut off fuel at the source, disconnect the nozzle, replace the SPR dust cap, remove grounding/bonding wires, and close door No. 8 without catching the dust cap chain.

records.query: State what action is required when a leak develops during refueling or defueling, and detail the emergency shutdown procedure to be followed.
records.reference: When a leak develops during refueling or defueling, stop all operations immediately. The emergency shutdown procedure is as follows: 1. Release the deadman control and pull the lanyard or control cable on the Type II hydrant system. If fuel continues to flow, actuate the nearest emergency fuel shutoff switch. 2. Actuate any of the emergency engine shutdown switches to stop the vehicle engine. 3. If the vehicle must be moved without stowing the servicing hoses or lowering the lift platform, close and disconnect the servicing nozzles and hydrant coupler, break the seal, and activate the interlock system override lever. 4. Close the hydrant coupler valve and the single-point nozzle valves. 5. Evacuate the area if instructed by maintenance or fire department personnel.
records.answer:
ACTION REQUIRED: If a leak develops during refueling or defueling, stop all operations. Take the necessary safety precautions and accomplish repairs before resuming operations (TO 00-25-172CL-5).

EMERGENCY SHUTDOWN PROCEDURE (refueling unit, TO 00-25-172CL-4):
During aircraft servicing, the refueling unit operator monitors the refueler for fuel leaks, ignition sources and other signs of malfunction. In an emergency:
a. Release deadman control.
b. Push engine auxiliary throttle control all the way in.
c. Turn off emergency switch.
d. Close hose reel shut off valve.
e. Close main tank emergency shut off valve.
f. Notify aircraft servicing supervisor, operations expediter and Fuels Control Center (FCC), if possible.
g. Evacuate area if instructed by servicing supervisor or fire department personnel.
NOTE: In case of a fuel spill other than normal aircraft venting, do not evacuate the fuel servicing vehicle until the area is declared safe by fire department personnel.

R-18/R-20 PUMPING UNIT VARIANT (TO 00-25-172CL-4): a. Release deadman and activate emergency shutdown switch on hand-held remote, R-18 pumping unit, or R-20 servicing platform. b. Close R-18 inlet valve and R-20 inlet valve (NOT the diverter valve V27). c. Notify aircraft servicing supervisor, operations expediter, and Fuels Service Center (FSC), if possible. d. Evacuate area if instructed by servicing supervisor or fire department personnel.

Note: Procedures for specific systems may differ slightly in wording; the general requirement is to stop all operations on leak discovery.

records.query: What signal is used to indicate hot brakes, and what is the first step if one is detected during inspection?
records.reference: The signal used to indicate hot brakes is to make a rapid fanning motion with one hand in front of the face while pointing to the wheel with the other hand during the day. At night, the signal is the same but with wands. The first step if hot brakes are detected during inspection is to check for hot brakes.
records.answer:
Signal: Hot brakes are signaled by a rapid fanning motion with one hand in front of the face, while pointing to the wheel with the other hand (day and night; at night the same is done with wands) per the Navy hand signals in TO 00-25-172CL-3.

First step when hot brakes are suspected or detected: Perform an aircraft hot brake check before proceeding, measuring brake temperature with temperature sensitive substances (temp sticks) or infrared heat sensors (TO 00-25-172). Fuel servicing does not start until brake temperature is below 750 °F (exempt aircraft: A-10, C-5, C-17, C-130, E-4, F-15, HH-60; F-22 may be refueled above 750 °F only with an adequate shield protecting the left main gear brake assembly). Aircraft with suspected or known hot brakes will not enter the hot refueling pad (TO 00-25-172, hot refueling sequence). CAUTION: temp sticks have damaged some brake assembly pressure plate antioxidant coatings; refer to MDS-specific TOs. Note: the pages do not give a general, non-refueling first step for hot brakes found during routine inspection; the procedure above is the one documented.
